evidence.quote: The DIW-based 3D printing was conducted with a 3D-Bioplotter (Envision TEC, Germany) with tapered polyethylene nozzles (with 410 μm tip opening, Nordson EFD). The orthogonal microlattices, with overall dimensions 9 × 9 × 13.5 mm3, were printed with a vertical layer thickness of 330 μm, a horizontal spacing of 1.125 mm between each strut, and a rotation angle of 90° between layers, as shown in Fig. 1a.
Green bodies were dried overnight and then sintered in three steps:
(i) evaporation of residual DCM and decomposition of PS at 400 °C for 1.5 h and at 550 °C for 4 h under flowing ultra-high purity (UHP) Ar (99.999 %) to remove organic materials in inks;
(ii) sintering at 1220 °C for 20 h in quartz capsules (20 kPa, UHP Ar) and;
(iii) aging at 850 °C for 50 h in the same quartz capsules to precipitate the γ’ phase.
the sintered demonstration objects were blasted for 15 or 60 s with glass beads (74–177 µm, Potters) in a sandblaster (Media Blast & Abrasive) using a pressure of 345 kPa.

Increasing the Ti concentration from 4 at% (Al9Co26Cr7Fe16Ni38Ti4) to 9 at% (Al8Co25Cr7Fe15Ni36Ti9) leads to a significant increase in the volume fraction of strengthening γ’ precipitates, from 51 to 78 %.
In the Ti-rich composition, the γ’ precipitates exhibit a sharp-edged cubic morphology with larger sizes and higher lattice misfit (0.63 %) with respect to the γ matrix.

Although the specimens were protected by flowing ultra-high purity Ar during the entire sintering process, several Al2O3 particles (white arrows in Fig. 3b, c, i) are observed, reflecting the high affinity of Al to oxygen at high temperatures
In the densest region of struts (white box, Fig. 3a), only micropores with sizes of ~1–3 μm are present, (yellow arrows, Fig. 3b).
Occasional larger pores with 10–15 μm sizes are visible in the less dense regions (blue box, Fig. 3a).
